title: The Treaty

jokes.text: Leslie reveals she has collected all 193 national flags and has them on hand immediately
jokes.setup: Leslie casually asks if Ben has seen her complete collection of all 193 national flags
jokes.punchline: 'Ooh! Here they are.' — they're right there, instantly produced, suggesting she carries them or has them absurdly accessible
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope character comedy — her over-preparation and intense dedication to civic activities is perfectly illustrated by owning all 193 flags. The immediate 'Ooh! Here they are' implies she either carries them or had them staged, which is funny but subtle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, have you seen my flag collection?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, there it is!

jokes.text: Ben: 'I kinda want to roll up my sleeves and make geopolitical problem-solving my bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ben is discussing Model UN country assignments with earnest enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: He describes geopolitical problem-solving in the language of a bro conquering a challenge, completely sincere
jokes.explanation: The contrast between 'geopolitical problem-solving' (bureaucratic, wonky) and 'make it my bitch' (aggressive bro-speak) is a sharp character joke. Ben's nerd-who-wants-to-be-cool energy is perfectly captured. Good economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to approach this with serious diplomatic strategy. It's about respect, decorum, and maintaining the highest standards of international relations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So we're gonna go in there and absolutely destroy those bitches.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Amen, brother.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just said he wants to 'make geopolitical problem-solving his bitch'
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds with total sincerity as if this is an inspiring rallying cry
jokes.explanation: Two words delivering a perfect reaction. Leslie matching Ben's mock-intensity with absolute sincerity is good character work. Economy is outstanding — the joke is entirely in the tone, not the words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I need you to represent Iceland in Model UN.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Iceland? The only countries I know are the ones from movies where they're villains.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, I can do Russia, North Korea, maybe some made-up Eastern European place. But Iceland? That's not a villain country. That's a place where people go to see the Northern Lights and feel feelings.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Iceland? The bad guys from Mighty Ducks 2? Don't think so.' / 'Japan? The bad guys from Karate Kid 2? Even worse.' / 'Germany? They've never been the bad guys.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to assign Andy a country for Model UN
jokes.punchline: Andy's cultural knowledge consists entirely of sports movie villains, culminating in the absurd 'Germany has never been the bad guys'
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open. The escalating structure is perfect: Iceland (Mighty Ducks 2) → Japan (Karate Kid 2) → Germany ('They've never been the bad guys'). The final beat is the killer — Andy's complete historical ignorance delivered with total conviction. The joke escalates and then pulls the rug. Highly quotable, perfectly characterizes Andy as lovably dumb. This comfortably reaches 8+ territory.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What about Germany?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Germany? No way. That's where all the bad guys are from.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, Germany is a wonderful country with rich culture and history.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, in movies. Every time there's Nazis or terrorists or evil robots, they're always German. I don't want to go somewhere like that.

jokes.text: Leslie offers Japan — Andy: 'The bad guys from Karate Kid 2? Even worse.'
jokes.setup: Established pattern from Iceland/Mighty Ducks 2
jokes.punchline: 'Even worse' — Andy has a hierarchy of sports movie villains, and Japan ranks lower than Iceland
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the running gag works brilliantly — 'even worse' implies Andy has a ranked hierarchy of movie villain countries. The callback amplifies the original joke and the logic is airtight within Andy's worldview. The escalation from 'don't think so' to 'even worse' is perfect comic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be the Moon.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, you can't be the Moon. The Moon isn't a country.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So? I'm still doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not how Model UN works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've made my decision, Leslie. I'm the Moon now.

jokes.text: April: 'I'll be the Moon.' / Leslie: 'No, you're gonna be South Africa or—' / April: 'Moon or quit, man.' / Leslie: 'Fine. You be South Africa, and you can also secretly run the moon.' / April: 'The Moon accepts your ridiculous proposal.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is assigning countries; April refuses any real country and insists on being the Moon
jokes.punchline: Leslie capitulates with the compromise that April is South Africa AND secretly runs the Moon; April accepts in full diplomatic register
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist character comedy. April's nihilistic refusal to engage with the premise is perfectly in character, and 'The Moon accepts your ridiculous proposal' is a brilliant button — April adopting the formal UN register to accept a completely unhinged arrangement. The phrase 'secretly run the moon' is inspired. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Andy, I've been thinking about your moon demand, and I want to find a compromise that works for both of us.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I appreciate that, Leslie, but I'm not sure The Moon is interested in compromises.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Moon? Andy, you are The Moon.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I am speaking on behalf of The Moon. The Moon accepts your compromise, provided it includes adequate lunar lighting for the town of Pawnee.

jokes.text: Ron: 'And teach kids that not only is government good but that there should be a World-wide super-government? I'd rather sand down my toenails.'
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically invites Ron to join Model UN, offering him America
jokes.punchline: Ron's libertarian objection escalates to a vivid and oddly specific alternative he'd prefer
jokes.explanation: Solid Ron Swanson character comedy. The objection to a 'World-wide super-government' is perfectly Ron, and 'I'd rather sand down my toenails' is a vivid, specific alternative that lands well. The setup immediately following makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm offering you the chance to play America in our historical reenactment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. America is a collective concept, Leslie. I don't do collectives. Also, I once tried to secede from a Rotary Club meeting by locking myself in the bathroom for six hours.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Every three weeks, I have to sand down my toenails. They're too strong for clippers.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just said he'd rather sand down his toenails than join Model UN
jokes.punchline: He clarifies, unprompted, that this is a real thing he does because his toenails are 'too strong for clippers'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. What seemed like hyperbole is revealed to be Ron's literal reality — his toenails are so strong they require sanding. The casual delivery of 'They're too strong for clippers' is perfectly deadpan. It's absurdist body horror wrapped in Ron's hyper-masculine matter-of-factness. Highly quotable, perfectly characterizes Ron, and the callback structure (the hyperbole becomes literal) is elegantly constructed. Justifies 8.5+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a high pain threshold. In fact, I didn't even feel the nail clippers break. I just realized I needed to switch to a Dremel.

jokes.text: Student fan recognizes Leslie and treats her like a celebrity: 'Are you Leslie Knope? Oh, what am I talking about? Of course you are.' / 'Bonjour, Madame Ambassadeur.'
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the high school Model UN
jokes.punchline: A teenager greets her with the reverence normally reserved for an actual world leader or celebrity
jokes.explanation: Competent character comedy playing on Leslie's inflated local celebrity status. The French greeting is a nice touch. Functional but not exceptional — the joke is clear but doesn't have a sharp twist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm not a legend. I mean, I did win Best Delegate three years in a row, but that's not really a big deal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Although, if you want to call me a Model UN deity or a parliamentary goddess, I won't stop you.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I really wouldn't describe myself as a Model U.N. legend.' / Student: 'I'd go with icon. Or hero.'
jokes.setup: The student calls Leslie a Model UN legend; Leslie deflects with false modesty
jokes.punchline: The student immediately escalates to even grander titles
jokes.explanation: Good setup/punchline with nice economy. Leslie's false modesty punctured by the student going even bigger is a solid reversal. The beat works because it's also what Leslie secretly thinks of herself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Enron had the right idea. They just need better PR. I'm telling you, if they rebrand, maybe change the name to something like 'Enron 2.0' or 'New Enron,' people would totally invest again. It's all about the comeback narrative.

jokes.text: Tom's jargon-heavy self-promotion: 'E720 going under was a blessing. I'm tearing it up all over town like a boss.'
jokes.setup: Tom is being interviewed by Ron for his old job but insists he doesn't need it
jokes.punchline: Tom uses inflated entrepreneur-speak to describe what is clearly a failing situation
jokes.explanation: Functional Tom character comedy — his bravado masking failure is a well-established bit for this character. 'Like a boss' is a bit dated even for the era. Works as setup for the Macy's reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom's become quite the entrepreneur. Started his own business, made millions.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Last I saw him, he was at Macy's handing out samples of Swedish meatballs.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'I've offered Tom his job back several times, and each time he's told me he's just too busy being an entrepreneur. Then two days ago, I saw him spraying cologne samples at Macy's. The young man has a lot of pride.'
jokes.setup: Ron recounts Tom's repeated refusals to return to his old job, citing entrepreneurial success
jokes.punchline: Ron personally witnessed Tom working a sample counter at Macy's, and describes this with dry sympathy: 'The young man has a lot of pride.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent deadpan confessional. The structure is perfect: Ron builds up Tom's excuses, then deflates them with a single concrete image (spraying cologne at Macy's), then adds the kicker 'The young man has a lot of pride' — which is both sympathetic and withering at once. Ron's dry delivery makes this land much harder than it reads. Near-excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I feel like we really connected on the dance floor.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You looked like a newborn giraffe learning to walk.

jokes.text: Ann's sarcastic advice about Chris's relationship: 'Wow. A four-date-long relationship might not be 100% perfect? I think you should launch a full-scale investigation.'
jokes.setup: Chris dramatically tells Ann his four-date relationship is 'in trouble' and he doesn't know why
jokes.punchline: Ann responds with withering sarcasm, mocking the absurdity of treating this like a crisis
jokes.explanation: Good sarcasm with solid structure. Ann's exasperated reaction to Chris treating a four-date relationship like a state emergency is relatable and well-timed. The 'full-scale investigation' phrase is funny because it's exactly what Chris will then do.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why don't you just break up with her? I mean, she disagreed with you about one thing. That's basically infidelity.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You should probably move to a new city and start a new life under an assumed name.

jokes.text: Chris: 'The root of sarcasm is truth, Ann. I am going to launch a full-scale investigation. And I sincerely thank you for that suggestion.'
jokes.setup: Ann has sarcastically suggested a 'full-scale investigation'; she clarifies it was sarcasm
jokes.punchline: Chris genuinely takes it as wise advice, philosophizes about sarcasm, and commits to the investigation with sincere gratitude
jokes.explanation: Great Chris Traeger character comedy. His relentless positivity and inability to register sarcasm is perfectly deployed here. 'The root of sarcasm is truth' sounds like something he'd have on a motivational poster. The sincere thank-you is the button. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, we should probably launch a full investigation into this.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You're right, we should. I'll get my notebook and we can set up a task force. I'm thinking weekly meetings, maybe some flow charts.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Glad I could help in these trying times.' Chris: 'Sarcasm again! You're a delight.'
jokes.setup: Ann makes another sarcastic comment
jokes.punchline: Chris correctly identifies it as sarcasm this time but responds with genuine warmth and delight
jokes.explanation: Nice button on the previous joke — Chris now identifies the sarcasm but still responds with warmth, showing his positivity is unassailable. 'You're a delight' is perfectly Chris. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: With Ben, it's deeper than romance. It's friendship. It's trust. It's knowing that no matter what happens, he's got my back. Romance is just 'I love you, let's get married.' Friendship is forever.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head about friendship vs. romance: 'Friends help you move. They drive you to the airport. Boyfriends just... love you and marry you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is rationalizing why friendship with Ben is better than dating him
jokes.punchline: She lists friendship perks as superior to romantic love and marriage, which she dismisses with 'just'
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed talking-head joke. The list of friendship perks (moving, airport) sounds like Leslie's genuine prioritization, and then 'Boyfriends just... love you and marry you' — with the devastating 'just' doing all the work — reveals the denial underneath. The pause before 'love you' suggests she knows how absurd it sounds. Highly quotable, emotionally resonant, structurally elegant. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Donna, I need dating advice. Should I call Ann or should I wait for her to call me?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Dangle carrots both ways. Call her on Monday, wait for her to call you on Tuesday. By Wednesday, she won't know which end is up.

jokes.text: Chris interrupts Jerry at his own desk to launch a romantic investigation, with Donna pulled in: 'Jerry! I am launching a full-scale investigation into my romantic relationship with your daughter Millicent Gergich, and I thought I could pick your brain.'
jokes.setup: Chris has decided to interrogate Jerry about his own daughter's feelings
jokes.punchline: The sheer inappropriateness of asking a father to help decode why his daughter stopped calling you — delivered with complete Chris sincerity
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'full-scale investigation' pays off well. The awkwardness of Chris cornering Jerry about his own daughter is good cringe comedy. Jerry's 'Aw, jeez, I really shouldn't be involved' is perfectly Jerry. The joke is in the social inappropriateness Chris is completely blind to.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie or Ron
dialogue.line: So you retired in 1968?

dialogue.speaker: Courtney
dialogue.line: Yes, I had to leave after I told my secretary she had a nice ass. She was Black.

dialogue.speaker: Courtney
dialogue.line: Different times, you know?

jokes.text: Donna pulls in on command: 'Here's what I saw go down. Donna! Yeah! Get in on this.'
jokes.setup: Chris is consulting Jerry about his daughter; Donna is nearby
jokes.punchline: Chris immediately co-opts Donna with the enthusiasm of someone assembling an Ocean's Eleven team for a relationship problem
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — the absurdity of treating this like a crisis operation is consistent with Chris's character. Donna's immediate availability and willingness adds to the comedy. Not particularly sharp on its own.

jokes.text: Donna's advice: 'You're too accessible. Every time she calls, you answer. You gotta dangle the carrot, literally and metaphorically.'
jokes.setup: Chris has assembled a team to diagnose his relationship problem
jokes.punchline: 'Dangle the carrot, literally and metaphorically' — Donna delivers relationship advice with the same confidence she uses for everything, adding 'literally' in a way that raises questions
jokes.explanation: The 'literally and metaphorically' tag is the joke — what does it mean to literally dangle a carrot in a dating context? Donna delivers it as if it's obvious, which is classic Donna. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you can't just call someone racist during a job interview!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I didn't call them racist. I said their tie was a racist tie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That doesn't make it better, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a perfectly good tie. I don't see what the problem is.

jokes.text: Job interview: Courtney reveals he was fired in 1968 for making a pass at 'an ethnic woman,' has been hitchhiking since, went to Mexico, 'met a lot of ethnic girls,' went to jail, 'and that about brings it up to date.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tom are interviewing candidates to replace Tom as administrator
jokes.punchline: The candidate calmly recounts 43 years of racist, criminal wandering as if summarizing a resume; Tom delivers the button 'Sounds to me like you're ready to get back in the game, Courtney'
jokes.explanation: Dark cringe comedy — the joke is in Courtney's casual delivery of genuinely awful content, and Tom's oblivious button. The repeated 'ethnic' is the show leaning into discomfort deliberately. Gets a laugh but is uncomfortable by design. The Ron reaction (visible horror) is part of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been working on some innovative abbreviations to streamline our department communications. For example, instead of saying 'Parks and Recreation Department,' I've shortened it to 'PARD.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, that's just... the same length.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I made it 'Please Always Remember Doing' which is longer and means something completely different now.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction: 'Are you insane? He was a million-year-old racist! He said he liked ethnic girls, Tom.'
jokes.setup: Tom calls Courtney 'a very strong candidate'
jokes.punchline: Ron — himself a man of strong conservative views — is genuinely appalled, with 'million-year-old racist' being a vivid and funny descriptor
jokes.explanation: 'Million-year-old racist' is a vivid, funny, and perfectly economical phrase. The joke that Ron — a man who hates government and once gifted himself a steak — is the voice of reason here is good character comedy. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As Denmark, I have to say, you Americans really over-exaggerate everything. We Danes prefer to under-exaggerate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just made that word up. I'm very smart.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'In my four years here, I revolutionized the position of administrator and made this place cool. I was the first person to abbreviate Parks and Recreation Department. First it was Parks and Recreation. Then Parks and Rec. Then P&R. Then lengthened it just a little bit to... Tommy's place.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining his legacy at the Parks department
jokes.punchline: His 'revolution' in abbreviation ends with expanding back to 'Tommy's place' — a completely self-serving renaming that was obviously never official
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation. The series P&R → Parks and Rec → Parks and Recreation → P&R creates a logical compression pattern, then 'lengthened just a little bit to Tommy's place' is a perfect subversion — longer, completely self-promotional, definitely unofficial. The structure IS the joke. Highly Tom-specific. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie and I are just having fun. We're keeping it fun. It's fun.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Very fun. So much fun.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Fun, fun, fun, fun, fun.

jokes.text: Model UN student: 'Under-exaggerate much, France? Ha ha!'
jokes.setup: Model UN students are doing their best diplomacy; one chastises France
jokes.punchline: A high schooler says 'under-exaggerate' with total confidence — a malapropism for 'understate'
jokes.explanation: Mild background joke — a student using 'under-exaggerate' incorrectly while trying to sound diplomatic. Not a strong joke on its own but adds texture to the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I negotiated a peace treaty between two warring nations by trading their entire military for a pride of lions.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the worst deal in the history of deals.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, no — they were really into it. Lions are majestic.

jokes.text: Ben's reaction talking head: 'Leslie and I aren't dating anymore, but, uh, we're friends. So it's fun. It's just fun. It's fun... it's... fun...'
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining that their friendship is fine and fun
jokes.punchline: His repetition of 'fun' becomes increasingly hollow and strained, the word losing all meaning as he convinces himself
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe talking-head. The camera holding on Ben as he repeats 'fun' with diminishing conviction is deeply relatable and funny. Parks and Rec excels at these small character moments. The visual of Ben's face deflating is implied and lands hard.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Lions will kill you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But they're free.

jokes.text: Cut from Ben's deflating 'fun' confessional directly to him forcing cheer: 'It is fun. Thanks a lot.'
jokes.setup: Ben's talking head ends on a defeated note
jokes.punchline: A cut to the next scene where Ben overcorrects with performed cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke using the edit. The transition from confessional misery to performed okayness is a classic mockumentary move, and Ben's character makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My strategy is simple: I'm going to accumulate as many lions as possible. Everyone knows that whoever has the most lions wins Model UN.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've already started my lion collection. I have zero lions, but by the end of this, I'm going to have... way more than zero.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Honey! I just traded Finland's military to Kenya for 50 lions. That's pretty good, right?' April: 'Yeah...' Andy: 'But also militaries are pretty good at protecting countries.' April: 'But so are lions. And you don't have to pay them.'
jokes.setup: Andy has made a diplomatic trade in Model UN
jokes.punchline: He traded Finland's entire military for 50 lions; April, rather than correcting him, endorses the lion strategy with 'you don't have to pay them'
jokes.explanation: Delightful absurdist character comedy. Andy's geopolitical strategy (lions > military) is perfectly dumb, and April's endorsement of it — with the logical but equally absurd 'you don't have to pay them' — makes it a two-person bit. Their relationship is perfectly captured in two people agreeing that lions are a valid military strategy. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, can you wrap this up in like 10 or 15 minutes?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. 40 minutes. Got it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, 10 or 15.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, 40 minutes, I'm on it.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional: 'I've just traded all of Finland's boring stuff for every other country's lions? I definitely have more lions than any other country in the whole world right now. I have no idea what's going on. But if that ends up meaning something in this game, I'd say I'm set.'
jokes.setup: Andy is summarizing his Model UN strategy
jokes.punchline: His entire strategy is lion accumulation, he admits he has no idea what's happening, but is confident this will matter somehow
jokes.explanation: Excellent follow-through on the lion bit. 'I have no idea what's going on. But if that ends up meaning something in this game, I'd say I'm set.' is perfect Andy logic — blissful ignorance paired with unfounded confidence. Character integration is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Your life is so awesome. You're married to Ben Wyatt, you have perfect hair, and you work in government.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, thank you. That's very nice of you to say.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna be just like you when I grow up.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, you're not! You're gonna work at a call center and you're gonna like it!

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ben to 'tread water' while she does a photo op; Ben says 'I'll just tread water until you're ready. Thanks, buddy.' with increasing strain in his voice.
jokes.setup: Leslie casually asks Ben to pause their joint Model UN work for her campaign photo op
jokes.punchline: Ben repeats 'tread water' back to her with the careful tone of someone choosing not to say what they're really feeling
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — the subtext is doing heavy lifting. 'Thanks, buddy' from Ben is quietly devastating given his feelings. The comedy is in what's not being said.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am speaking Danish. Jeg er meget glad. Jeg elsker dig.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's just English.

jokes.text: Ben asks for 'five more minutes' on the photo op, Leslie says '10 or 15 to be safe,' then 'How about we make it a cool 40?' — escalating delays as Ben treads water
jokes.setup: Ben thought the photo op would be quick; Leslie keeps extending it
jokes.punchline: From 5 → 10 or 15 → 'a cool 40' — the casual escalation of 'a cool 40' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: 'A cool 40' is a funny specific — the casualness of 'cool' applied to a 40-minute wait. The escalation structure is clean. Leslie's obliviousness to Ben's situation adds cringe depth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I come before you today in my capacity as Deputy Director of the Parks Department to formally request that we change the name of Ramsett Park to something less stupid.

jokes.text: Student (Bulgaria) to Ben, staring at Leslie with envy: 'Her life is so awesome. You're lucky you're friends with her.' Ben: 'Shut up, Bulgaria!'
jokes.setup: A random student is expressing admiration for Leslie to Ben — unaware of their complicated relationship
jokes.punchline: Ben, clearly pained, snaps 'Shut up, Bulgaria!' — his frustration displaced onto a child and a country
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Shut up, Bulgaria!' perfectly captures Ben's emotional state — he's in pain, he can't say anything real, and his only outlet is snapping at a teenager representing Bulgaria. The specificity of the country name makes it absurdly funny. Highly quotable, great economy, earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You can't be friends with someone after you've been romantic with them. It just doesn't work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because you know each other's bodies. You've seen things. You can't unsee them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, we've been friends for years. We've seen each other's bodies. I've seen you in a bathing suit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's different.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How is that different? You have a body. I have a body. We both have bodies.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Or, as they say in Denmark... "I'm back."' Leslie: 'Most people speak English.'
jokes.setup: Ben has been playing Denmark; he returns with a joke about speaking Danish
jokes.punchline: Leslie deflates it instantly — Denmark is predominantly English-speaking enough to make the affectation pointless
jokes.explanation: Brisk, efficient joke. Ben tries a bit; Leslie kills it immediately. The economy of Leslie's response is the whole joke. Quick and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is not just a Model UN situation anymore. This is a declaration of war. I am formally declaring war on the country of Bahrain. And I'm doing it in a high school exercise, which makes it extra official.

jokes.text: Ben discovers he's been cut out of his own treaty: 'I got cut out of my own treaty?' / Leslie: 'Yeah. I got sick of treading water, so I swam over to Asia, made a deal.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Leslie to wait; she instead negotiates a competing treaty
jokes.punchline: Leslie's casual use of the 'tread water / swim' metaphor — now weaponized — is both a callback and a reveal of her competitive nature
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Leslie's 'I swam over to Asia' repurposes Ben's 'tread water' language as a punchline. Also functions as a character reveal: even in a model UN, Leslie's competitive instincts override friendship. Solid structure.

dialogue.speaker: Job Applicant
dialogue.line: So I was at the grocery store last week, and I picked up a gallon of milk. It was 2% milk. Do you know what that means?

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: No, what?

dialogue.speaker: Job Applicant
dialogue.line: It means 98% of the milk is missing. I've been paying for milk that's mostly not there. Anyway, I think that's pretty interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: ...You're hired.

jokes.text: Ben in full diplomatic register: 'The nation of Denmark would like to formerly request a summit with the nation of Peru over there by the refreshment table. Because the nation of Denmark needs a juice box.'
jokes.setup: Ben is furious at Leslie but they're in a high school Model UN
jokes.punchline: He channels his anger into the formal diplomatic language of the game, only to reveal the summit is because he needs a juice box
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The contrast between the formal UN language ('The nation of Denmark would like to formerly request') and the absurd need ('Because the nation of Denmark needs a juice box') is perfectly constructed. 'Formerly' instead of 'formally' may also be an intentional character error. The structure holds the formality all the way through the setup before releasing on 'juice box.' Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Gary, you can't just make up stories about yourself. Like, I could say I once bench-pressed a horse, but that didn't happen.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Well, I wasn't making it up...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Gary, you told us you went skydiving last month. We all watched you nearly pass out when the chair broke.

jokes.text: Ben breaks character to confront Leslie at the refreshment table, the Model UN dissolving into a proxy argument for their actual relationship
jokes.setup: Ben has been trying to maintain the fiction that friendship is fine
jokes.punchline: He snaps and uses 'diplomatic language' as cover to say exactly how he feels, making the Model UN the most emotionally loaded juice box summit in history
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a real emotional confrontation disguised within Model UN diplomatic speak is a sustained bit that works well. This beat sets up the escalation to come.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Keith, this is your job application. Question 3 asks 'What are your weaknesses?' and you wrote 'My parents.'

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: Well, it's true.

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: '...I've shared my flags with him, and suddenly, he doesn't want to be friends?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is listing her grievances with Ben's behavior
jokes.punchline: The flag-sharing is presented as a significant emotional investment — because for Leslie, it genuinely is
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the opening. Leslie's flags are a recurring symbol of her earnestness, and sharing them is, in her world, a gesture of deep friendship. The joke works because the audience understands the sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: I want to be a mid-level bureaucrat with a secure job and good benefits. That's it. I don't want to be a director or anything. I just want to show up, do my job competently, and go home.

jokes.text: Leslie, as Denmark, formally declares war on Peru: 'Attention. This is an urgent world matter. Due to a recent betrayal, my homeland, the great state of Denmark, has officially decided to declare war on Peru.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie's personal conflict has been simmering through the Model UN
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses the model UN as a literal theater of war for her personal grievances, escalating to a full war declaration against Ben/Peru
jokes.explanation: Great escalation moment. Leslie's competitive and emotional intensity channeled into Model UN war is perfectly in character. 'The great state of Denmark' is a small but funny geographic error. The scene perfectly merges the A-plot and B-plot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Maybe you should wave a white flag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A white flag? Ben, I'm going to take that flag, wrap it around a rock, and throw it through their window. Then I'm going to climb through that window, grab them by the collar, and drag them back here.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Scandinavian brothers, on my signal. Unleash hell!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has declared war; she's Denmark in a high school Model UN
jokes.punchline: She deploys a Gladiator quote in full earnest seriousness to command her Model UN coalition
jokes.explanation: Brilliant button on the war declaration. 'Unleash hell' is the Gladiator line, delivered with complete sincerity at a high school Model UN. The contrast between the grandiosity of the phrase and the context is perfect. 'Scandinavian brothers' is also funny — Denmark would have, at most, Norway and Sweden.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom was perfect for the job. His business idea for 'Tommy Trees' — a chain of stores selling tiny trees for tiny people — showed exactly the kind of ambition and lack of self-awareness we needed.

jokes.text: Chris's talking head: 'See, I just don't believe in this whole don't let people know how you feel nonsense. I love telling people how I feel. Mostly because I love most people. And I love telling them that I love them.'
jokes.setup: Chris is philosophizing about emotional openness
jokes.punchline: His declaration of love for everyone is so expansive it becomes absurd — and sets up the next beat
jokes.explanation: Good Chris character comedy — his relentless positivity articulated with genuine conviction. The joke is in the recursive logic: he loves people, so he loves telling them he loves them. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can't go back to my old job. You know why? Because I'm like a shark.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A shark has to keep moving forward, or it dies. And I have to keep moving forward, or I die.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's the same thing.

jokes.text: Ann's check: 'You didn't tell that girl you love her, did you?' Chris: 'No. I'm not crazy.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just declared he loves telling people he loves them
jokes.punchline: Ann has to check; Chris's response shows rare self-awareness, which is itself funny
jokes.explanation: Sharp two-line joke. The setup is Chris's previous speech; Ann's concern is warranted; Chris's 'No. I'm not crazy' is funny because of course we believe he might have. The economy is near-perfect — nine words deliver the full joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: If you don't join Leslie's coalition, I'm gonna tell the Moon to stop doing the tides, and then you'll all drown.

jokes.text: Job interview: Gary from Gary, Indiana. 'My name's Gary, and I'm from Gary, Indiana. Amazing. People like hearing that. It's probably one of my stronger anecdotes.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ron are interviewing more candidates
jokes.punchline: A man named Gary considers 'I'm from Gary, Indiana' to be one of his stronger anecdotes — a fact, not an anecdote, and not interesting regardless
jokes.explanation: Good structured joke. The comedy is in Gary's complete lack of self-awareness about what constitutes an anecdote or interesting content. 'It's probably one of my stronger anecdotes' is the killer phrase — the self-assessment of pride is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris and I are going to this amazing bed and breakfast upstate. They have a chocolate body paint experience.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Body paint? That sounds messy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's supposed to be very romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I once knew a woman who covered herself in liverwurst. Worst six minutes of my life.

jokes.text: Tom: 'A fact is not an anecdote, Gary. Here's an anecdote... Today I met the most boring man in the world. His name was Gary.'
jokes.setup: Gary has called his name/hometown a strong anecdote
jokes.punchline: Tom demonstrates what an anecdote is by creating one about Gary — which is a devastating insult delivered as a grammar lesson
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is exceptional: Tom corrects Gary's terminology, then immediately demonstrates the correct usage with a sentence that destroys Gary. 'A fact is not an anecdote / Today I met the most boring man in the world. His name was Gary.' — the parallelism, the pivot, and the ruthless efficiency make this a standout line. Fully justifies 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: This is worse than the real UN.

jokes.text: Keith's job application: Under sex, wrote 'Yes. Ha ha, ha ha, ha ha.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ron are reviewing another candidate's application
jokes.punchline: 'Under sex, you wrote... Yes. Ha ha, ha ha, ha ha.' — a classic joke about the sex/gender form field, with the written laughter included
jokes.explanation: This is an old, well-worn joke — the sex/gender form field response. What saves it slightly is including the written 'ha ha, ha ha, ha ha' and Ron's 'Well-played' / Keith's 'Thank you' exchange. Still pretty hacky in concept but executed with some charm.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You should talk to Ben. He's been taking sadness baths.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Well-played.' Keith: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Keith has written 'Yes. Ha ha, ha ha' on the sex line of his application
jokes.punchline: Ron, of all people, salutes the joke with 'Well-played' and Keith accepts the compliment graciously
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'Well-played' — completely deadpan, entirely sincere — is more charming than the original joke. The exchange between two characters giving each other genuine respect for a dumb joke is funnier than the joke itself.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris is so obsessed with being healthy and perfect that he's basically dating a version of himself.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Which explains why their relationship is just them comparing fitness trackers and talking about their morning jogs.

jokes.text: Keith: 'What am I hoping to get out of this job? Yeah. Like one... one month of money... Would be... would be just right.'
jokes.setup: Tom poses the interview question: what are you hoping to get out of this job?
jokes.punchline: Keith's answer is startling in its honesty — just one month of money — delivered with the careful deliberation of someone who genuinely hasn't considered working longer
jokes.explanation: Good anti-interview comedy. Keith's refreshingly honest and catastrophically bad answer — 'one month of money' — is funny because of its specificity and the halting way he arrives at it. The pauses imply genuine deliberation.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris completely changed my life. He got me into jogging, and now I run every morning at 5 AM. I've never been in better shape. But I have to say, I've lost all my friends, my social life is completely gone, and I'm basically a shell of a human being. So... worth it?

jokes.text: Tom: 'Let me give you a situation. You're hosting a town hall meeting for local businesses.' Keith: 'Uh... That's so much stuff.' Tom: 'You just, uh... kept on going.' Keith: 'That was like one thing.' Tom: 'I didn't even get to the situation yet.'
jokes.setup: Tom begins a hypothetical interview scenario
jokes.punchline: Keith is overwhelmed before Tom finishes the setup; Tom points out he hasn't even described the actual situation yet
jokes.explanation: Strong escalating interview joke. Keith tapping out at 'you're hosting a town hall meeting' while Tom notes he hasn't even gotten to the scenario is a perfectly timed two-beat joke. 'That was like one thing' vs. 'I didn't even get to the situation yet' is great back-and-forth.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so 'Eagleton' is an anagram of 'leg tone'?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, Andy, that's not what an anagram is.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I'm pretty sure it is. E-L-E-G-T-O-N... leg tone.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not even close to how anagrams work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm sticking with leg tone.

jokes.text: Keith's exit confessional: 'Still not totally sure what I'm applying for. But... if you ask me, I think it went pretty well.'
jokes.setup: Keith has just bombed an interview spectacularly
jokes.punchline: He has no idea what the job is and thinks it went well
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Keith interview sequence. His combined ignorance and misplaced confidence is a reliable comedy formula but executed with good economy here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, how do you know about the Treaty of Westphalia?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, my buddy Derek told me about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your friend Derek knows about 17th century diplomacy?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, he was explaining how his backyard borders his neighbor's property. He called it the Treaty of West-failure because they keep fighting about the fence line.

jokes.text: Leslie trying to redirect the Model UN: 'Global politics can change, and scenarios can arise and suddenly you're just like, "wait, I thought this one thing, but look over there. That's a different thing, and it's changing everything," and I'm like, "what? Hold up." Who has tanks for me?'
jokes.setup: Students protest that Leslie is changing the food crisis scenario to a war against Peru
jokes.punchline: Leslie's non-explanation for why scenarios change is pure word salad, ending with a practical request for tanks
jokes.explanation: Fun Leslie moment — her attempt to justify her irrational behavior with diplomatic hand-waving is perfectly in character. The pivot to 'Who has tanks for me?' is a good button. Slightly long but serves its purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what would really appeal to teenage boys? A skateboard park.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! We could call it 'Radical Larry's House of Extreme Thrills and Soft Pretzels.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not... that's not what I meant.

jokes.text: April: 'Say the word, Leslie. I'll sick my army of lions on him.'
jokes.setup: April is supporting Leslie's war effort
jokes.punchline: April's weapon of choice — the lion army she and Andy accumulated — is offered as a legitimate threat
jokes.explanation: The callback to the lion subplot pays off beautifully here. April offering the lion army as a serious military resource connects two previously separate joke threads. 'Sick my army of lions on him' is extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron! I can explain. This isn't what it looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're wearing a Macy's employee uniform.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, yes, but I'm not actually working here. I'm just wearing this uniform to understand the retail experience from the inside. For research. My fragrance division needs authentic insights.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're folding shirts.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. And let me tell you, the way I fold these shirts is revolutionary. Look at this crease. Flawless. This is museum-quality folding. I'm basically an artist.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'God, it's time for you to nut up, Switzerland.'
jokes.setup: Switzerland (a student) is trying to stay neutral in the Denmark-Peru conflict
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses aggressive slang to bully a high schooler playing Switzerland into taking her side in her personal vendetta
jokes.explanation: Sharp one-liner. 'Nut up, Switzerland' is funny because it (1) breaks the Model UN register, (2) accurately represents Switzerland's geopolitical reputation for neutrality, and (3) comes from an adult bullying teenagers. The specificity of Switzerland makes this better than a generic insult.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the most beautiful room in the entire world. If you took the Sistine Chapel, the Taj Mahal, and the Eiffel Tower, and combined them into one room, it would be about 40% as nice as this council chamber.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Oh, you know what? You might wanna borrow this.' / Leslie: 'Ew, no one wants your dirty underwear, Ben.' / Ben: 'It's not dirty underwear. It's a white flag, and you may as well start waving it right now...' / Leslie: 'the only thing I will be waving is your decapitated head on a stick in front of your weeping mother!'
jokes.setup: Ben offers Leslie something white; she assumes it's underwear
jokes.punchline: Ben clarifies it's a surrender flag; Leslie's counter-threat escalates to graphic medieval violence — in a high school Model UN
jokes.explanation: 'The only thing I will be waving is your decapitated head on a stick in front of your weeping mother!' is a spectacular escalation. The underwear misdirection works as a quick beat before the real payoff. Leslie's threat is graphic, specific, and completely over-the-top for the context. This is one of the most quotable lines in the episode. The character integration is excellent — this is absolutely something Leslie Knope would say in a competitive situation. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, passion is what separates us from the animals. It's what makes us human. With passion, you can accomplish anything. You can move mountains, you can change lives, you can inspire people. Passion improves everything — art, music, sports, relationships, even wars.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'Tom Haverfords don't grow on trees. If they did, I'd sell 'em. Tommy trees.'
jokes.setup: Ron is reflecting on his inability to find a replacement for Tom
jokes.punchline: He immediately imagines a business opportunity from the hypothetical of Tom Haverfords growing on trees — 'Tommy trees'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke. 'Tommy trees' is delivered with complete deadpan finality — Ron's entrepreneurial instinct taking over even in a sentimental moment about a colleague. The brevity is perfect. Two words ('Tommy trees') that say everything about Ron. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: This copier is making too much noise. My ears are ringing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, I need to make copies. Your comfort is not my concern right now.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm like a shark. I don't swim backwards.' (Dramatic exit; then immediately returns to ask for his job back.)
jokes.setup: Tom delivers a dramatic self-comparison to a shark as he refuses to return
jokes.punchline: The episode reveals this was immediately followed by Tom returning to beg for his job
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Tom's grand exit is undercut by the episode's structure. The shark metaphor is both funny in itself (sharks do swim backwards... or don't, either way it's Tom being portentous) and ironic given what follows.

jokes.text: Leslie seizes the microphone from another delegate mid-speech: 'I move that the Security Council formally condemn Denmark...' Student: 'I'm not finished.' Leslie: 'Oh, really? Then why do I have the microphone?'
jokes.setup: A student is giving a speech; Leslie interrupts to push her personal agenda
jokes.punchline: 'Then why do I have the microphone?' — Leslie uses possession of the object as argument for legitimacy
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical line. 'Then why do I have the microphone?' uses unassailable kindergarten logic in a diplomatic context. Leslie as both teacher and participant who breaks every rule she's supposed to uphold is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Leslie after Denmark is condemned: 'That's no problemo, Peru, because Denmark no longer recognizes the authority of this international gang of thugs.'
jokes.setup: The Security Council has formally condemned Denmark
jokes.punchline: Leslie refuses to accept the ruling and reframes the UN as a 'gang of thugs'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's 'international gang of thugs' for the Model UN is a good escalation beat. She's now operating in full geopolitical paranoia mode. 'That's no problemo' is also a funny register break.

jokes.text: April's Moon joins Leslie's coalition: 'The Moon shall join your coalition.' Leslie: 'Yeah! We got the freaking moon. What are you gonna do without tides, Peru?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is seeking members for her Coalition of the Willing
jokes.punchline: The Moon (April) joins; Leslie immediately weaponizes tidal control as a geopolitical threat
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff for April's earlier insistence on being the Moon — it was setup for this moment. 'What are you gonna do without tides, Peru?' is both geographically absurd (Peru is landlocked in large parts and also has a coast, but tides as a weapon is ridiculous) and perfectly logical within the episode's internal absurdist rules. The callback structure makes this one of the best jokes in the episode. Earns 8.4+.

jokes.text: April, as the Moon, joining Leslie's coalition: 'The Moon shall join your coalition.' Andy: 'Yeah! We got the freaking moon. What are you gonna do without tides, Peru?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has formed the 'Coalition of the Willing' against Peru
jokes.punchline: The Moon joins — and Andy immediately frames lunar membership as a real threat ('What are you gonna do without tides, Peru?')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best payoffs. The Moon subplot (April's absurd demand) and the geopolitical war plot converge perfectly. 'What are you gonna do without tides, Peru?' is an exceptional line — Andy understands the physics of the Moon's influence on Earth and applies it as a military threat. Deeply quotable, high rewatch value, earns its score.

jokes.text: Ann: 'And the jacuzzi broke. But I did... eat food off of your body.' Chris: 'Oh, come on.' Jerry: 'All right, Chris and Ann!'
jokes.setup: Ann is recounting a relationship memory that started as a complaint
jokes.punchline: She admits to eating food off his body — in front of Jerry — which delights Donna and horrifies Chris, while Jerry just wants it to stop
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment. The specific detail 'eat food off of your body' is the funny element — it's not the most explicit thing but it's awkward enough, and Jerry's reaction ('All right, Chris and Ann!') is perfect Jerry. The audience-within-the-scene (Jerry and Donna) makes this funnier.

jokes.text: Andy's post-game: 'Did we win? I think we won! What were we trying to do? I learned so much today.'
jokes.setup: Denmark and Peru have been expelled; the Model UN is over
jokes.punchline: Andy has no idea what happened, thinks they won, and claims to have learned from the experience — without knowing what he learned
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy button. 'What were we trying to do? I learned so much today.' is textbook Andy Dwyer — boundless enthusiasm without any content. The escalating uncertainty ('Did we win? I think we won! What were we trying to do?') is beautifully structured. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Andy's advice to Leslie about talking to Ben: 'He takes really long sadness baths and makes me late for stuff.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to convince Leslie to make up with Ben
jokes.punchline: His motivation for wanting them to reconcile is purely logistical — Ben's sadness baths make Andy late
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. 'Sadness baths' is an inspired coinage — specific, visual, and immediately understandable as a depressed person ritual. The fact that Andy's concern for Leslie and Ben's relationship is entirely about his own scheduling is perfectly Andy. 'Really long sadness baths and makes me late for stuff' — the nonchalance, the specificity, the casualness about something that implies Ben is quite depressed. This is the kind of throwaway character detail that becomes a cultural touchstone. Economy is near-perfect. Fully justifies a score above 8.5.

jokes.text: Two random high school students having a sidebar: 'I hate it here. Can't wait to graduate.' / 'Yeah, but summer's gonna totally kick ass.'
jokes.setup: The Model UN has just imploded; students are reacting
jokes.punchline: Two students completely disengaged from the drama, talking about summer — a reminder of the actual context (a high school club)
jokes.explanation: Brief background joke — two students completely indifferent to the chaos around them. Grounds the scene in real high school energy. Not particularly sharp but adds texture and gets a mild smile.

jokes.text: Ann's revelation: 'I was so into you, okay, and you basically turned me into a female version of yourself, and then you got bored dating me because you were dating yourself.'
jokes.setup: Ann is getting real with Chris about why their relationship failed
jokes.punchline: The insight that Chris's relentless self-improvement made Ann into him, which then bored him, is sharp relationship psychology delivered as a comedic realization
jokes.explanation: Sharp character insight dressed as comedy. 'You got bored dating me because you were dating yourself' is a great line — it perfectly summarizes Chris's narcissism and explains the relationship failure in a genuinely witty way. High character integration and good structure.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I mean, I hate jogging.' Chris: 'Jogging's amazing!' Ann: 'Jogging is the worst, Chris. I mean, I know it keeps you healthy, but God, at what cost?' Chris: 'Well, I'm sorry that I added five years to your life.'
jokes.setup: Ann lists things she did for Chris that she hated, including jogging
jokes.punchline: Chris's defense — 'I'm sorry that I added five years to your life' — is a perfect blend of Chris-logic (fitness = years added) delivered with mock-apology
jokes.explanation: 'I'm sorry that I added five years to your life' is a quintessential Chris Traeger line — his worldview (everything healthy is a gift) is deployed defensively. The line is both character-specific and genuinely clever. Good economy and high character integration.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Now I'm being sarcastic. Like you. I'm doing something that you like.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just made a sarcastic comment and is announcing it
jokes.punchline: He announces his sarcasm explicitly and frames it as an act of affection/mimicry toward Ann
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the sarcasm running gag. Chris announcing his own sarcasm (because he now knows what it is) and framing it as a love language is a nice character evolution beat within the joke. Running gag pays off well here.

jokes.text: Andy: 'If you rearrange the letters of Peru, you could spell Europe.' Ben: 'That's... That's not true.' Andy: 'Well... You have to rearrange them.' Ben: 'Oh...'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to break the tension between Leslie and Ben with a fun fact
jokes.punchline: Peru does not contain the letters to spell Europe (it's missing an O and an E); Andy clarifies 'you have to rearrange them' as if the problem is the arrangement, not the letters
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier Andy Dwyer joke and one of the two or three best jokes in the episode. The setup is Andy trying to help with an interesting word game fact. The punchline is that it's not just wrong — it's fundamentally, impossibly wrong (Peru has 4 letters, Europe has 6; they don't share all letters). Andy's defense — 'Well... You have to rearrange them' — is perfect: he thinks the problem is that Ben is rearranging incorrectly, not that the letters don't exist. Ben's bewildered 'Oh...' is the button. This is Bertrand Russell levels of confident wrongness. Fully justifies 8.5+ score.

jokes.text: Andy's Camp David misunderstanding: 'In high school, my buddy David Fundis would have these campouts in his backyard... We called it camp David. How do you know about Camp David?'
jokes.setup: April suggests the summit could be Leslie and Ben's 'Camp David'
jokes.punchline: Andy thinks Camp David is a reference to his high school friend's backyard campouts, and is baffled/flattered that anyone knows about it
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Andy ignorance joke. The concept that Andy genuinely doesn't know Camp David is the presidential retreat — and assumes it's his own personal backyard tradition — is perfect. 'How do you know about camp David?' delivered with genuine surprise is the payoff. The joke escalates correctly: the setup is innocent-seeming, the explanation is increasingly ridiculous, and the button ('How do you know about camp David?') shows Andy has no idea he's exposed himself. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Andy and April exit to throw 'scientist bottles off the roof.' April: 'That's right. See ya. Go. Go. Go.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are looking for something to do while Leslie and Ben talk
jokes.punchline: Their plan is to throw 'scientist bottles' off the roof — a completely unexplained and absurd activity that April enthusiastically endorses
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist character beat. 'Scientist bottles' is a funny detail — what are those? Andy and April's relationship is perfectly captured in two people immediately agreeing to do something chaotic with zero explanation. April's 'That's right. See ya.' suggests she's been waiting for this.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie's treaty negotiation: 'I propose a treaty that states that we have a fun conversation once a day at work for five minutes.' / 'I'll take it to the Peruvian senate. Or whatever.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are genuinely trying to find a way to maintain their relationship
jokes.punchline: Leslie frames a five-minute daily chat as a formal international treaty; Ben accepts it in Peruvian diplomatic terms, then immediately breaks the register with 'Or whatever'
jokes.explanation: Warm, well-crafted joke that uses the episode's conceit (Model UN / treaties) to frame a genuine emotional moment. 'Or whatever' is the perfect deflation of Ben's maintained diplomatic façade. It's the moment real feeling breaks through the comedy.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'What do we do with those kids? We totally ruined their club.' Ben: 'I could tell you what I would like when I was their age.' Leslie: 'Ben, how are we gonna get Kathy Ireland to do naked aerobics for them?' Ben: 'Okay. I regret telling you that... very much.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are trying to think of how to make it up to the Model UN students
jokes.punchline: Ben's teenage fantasy (Kathy Ireland naked aerobics) has apparently been shared with Leslie previously, and she deploys it immediately and casually, mortifying him
jokes.explanation: Good joke — the specificity of 'Kathy Ireland doing naked aerobics' is funny (dated, specific, very Ben), and Leslie deploying this private information so casually and publicly is both funny and characterizes their intimacy. Ben's mortified 'very much' button is well-timed.

jokes.text: Tom's denial: 'What? Macy's? That wasn't me. There's a Macy's in town? Where's the Macy's in town? I heard they have an amazing cologne sample guy.'
jokes.setup: Ron confronts Tom about seeing him spraying cologne samples at Macy's
jokes.punchline: Tom first denies, then claims ignorance of the store, then immediately praises the cologne sample guy — in a sentence that collapses his denial
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Tom's denial collapses hilariously — he denies going to Macy's, claims not to know where it is, then immediately reveals he knows there's an 'amazing cologne sample guy' there, which is him. The self-incrimination in the third beat is perfectly structured. Tom's pride and his need to maintain dignity clash beautifully. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Ron begs the entire department to help him convince Tom to come back — including a dramatic 'I'm... begging.'
jokes.setup: Ron desperately needs Tom to return
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson — a man who has previously said he'd rather sand his own toenails than engage in government — publicly and visibly begs his colleagues for help, including the word 'begging'
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Ron Swanson begging is enormous because his character is defined by stoic self-sufficiency. His paused, pained delivery of 'I'm... begging' — with presumably a long, mortifying silence — is great character comedy. The visual of Ron in this state is implied and lands very hard. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ron gathers the entire Parks Department and begs them all to help convince Tom to return: 'Everyone, please... Help me. I'm trying to get Tom back. I'm... begging.'
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson — who never asks for help and considers vulnerability weakness — is publicly begging his entire staff
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson, the most proudly self-sufficient man alive, saying 'I'm... begging.' out loud to a room of people
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the character violation. Ron Swanson begging is a category error — it's like seeing a statue cry. His halting delivery ('I'm... begging.') suggests this is costing him physically. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Tom's response to Ron's begging: 'Ron, this is embarrassing. Even for you.' Then walks out.
jokes.setup: Ron has just performed an extraordinary act of public humiliation to convince Tom to return
jokes.punchline: Tom's criticism isn't that Ron begged — it's that it was done badly, 'even for you' suggesting Ron has done embarrassing things before
jokes.explanation: 'Even for you' is a perfect two-word addition that transforms a simple dismissal into a layered insult. Tom is so horrified by Ron's performance of begging that he can't engage with it. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Tom's response to Ron's public begging: 'Ron, this is embarrassing. Even for you.'
jokes.setup: Ron has humiliated himself publicly to get Tom back
jokes.punchline: 'Even for you' — implying Ron has a baseline level of embarrassing behavior, and this exceeds it
jokes.explanation: 'Even for you' is a great button — it implies a rich history of Ron-level embarrassments while also acknowledging this one is exceptional. Tom delivering it while he's the one being begged for adds irony.

jokes.text: Tom's scheme: He immediately tells Ron he plans to come back in a few days and have Ron beg again — then gets grabbed mid-sentence and pulled back.
jokes.setup: Tom has dramatically exited after dismissing Ron's begging
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he's negotiating — planning to extract more begging from Ron — but gets physically interrupted before he can finish explaining his scheme
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — Tom's dramatic exit is immediately undercut by his revelation that he was playing a long game. Being interrupted mid-scheme is a nice escalation that avoids explaining the joke too much. Very Tom to turn Ron's humiliation into a power play.

jokes.text: Tom asks for his job back with complete simplicity: 'Ron... May I have my job back, please?' Ron: 'Thank you. I will see you all Monday.'
jokes.setup: The entire elaborate arc of Tom's pride and Ron's begging has been building
jokes.punchline: Tom simply, quietly asks for his job back in the most basic terms; Ron accepts with equal simplicity — as if none of the preceding chaos happened
jokes.explanation: The comedy of the deflation — after all the theatrics, it ends with the plainest possible exchange. The economy here is the joke. Ron's satisfied 'Thank you' is particularly good; he's not gloating. Solid structural payoff.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Which, for the record, Denmark would have won, but that's neither here nor there.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are apologizing to the students for ruining the Model UN
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a genuine apology, Leslie cannot resist noting that Denmark would have won
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie moment. Her inability to let go of the competitive element even during an apology is completely in character. 'But that's neither here nor there' is the exactly right deflation after the competitive assertion. Highly character-specific.

jokes.text: Leslie's speech about passion: 'Passion is what makes for good treaties... Cheese! Good relationships... Good pizza. Good friends. Good everything. Including wars.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving an inspirational speech to the students about passion
jokes.punchline: Ben interrupts with 'Cheese!' as a passion example; Leslie incorporates it seamlessly; then ends the list with 'Including wars' — endorsing war as passion-driven
jokes.explanation: Good joke — Ben's interjection of 'Cheese!' mid-speech, Leslie absorbing it, and then ending with 'Including wars' as a positive thing on her passion list is a nice absurdist beat. The warmth of the scene makes the 'including wars' darker and funnier.

jokes.text: Tom's welcome-back celebration speech Ron attempts to deliver, struggling with the prepared remarks about Tom.
jokes.setup: Ron is giving what appears to be a prepared welcome-back speech for Tom
jokes.punchline: Ron clearly cannot bring himself to say the flattering things written; 'No, I'm not gonna say that' / 'All right, forget it' before pivoting to 'Welcome back, Tom Haverford!'
jokes.explanation: Strong Ron character comedy. His inability to read the flattering portions of Tom's welcome speech — audibly skipping lines — is perfectly Ron. The abandoned speech culminating in a bare 'Welcome back, Tom Haverford!' has the right structure. Ron's character integration is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Tom's re-entrance: 'Tick-tock, it's Tommy time!'
jokes.setup: Tom is officially welcomed back to the Parks Department
jokes.punchline: His catchphrase return is maximally Tom — brash, self-promotional, and immediately establishing dominance
jokes.explanation: Tom's catchphrase is character-specific and serves as a satisfying button to the arc. Not particularly original but delivers on character promise. 'Tick-tock, it's Tommy time' is absurd enough to be funny.

tmdb_overview: Leslie enlists the help of Ben, Andy and April to host a Model U.N. for Pawnee Central High School. Chris asks Ann for her advice on love when a date cancels on him. Meanwhile, Ron struggles to find a replacement for Tom.
insight: Native American treaty negotiation becomes deadpan gold at 1.94 jokes per minute.
